strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored and well-motivated gap: existing math/geometry benchmarks focus on high-level reasoning, while basic geometric perception (existence, counting, location, size, reference, relationship) is left largely unmeasured. The distinction is clearly articulated and empirically justified.

The benchmark is large-scale (80K images, 285K questions) and constructed via a fully automated, structured synthesis pipeline (Algorithm 1 + rendering + template QA generation), which supports scalability and precise, verifiable ground truth since figures are generated from known structured descriptions rather than collected/annotated.

Extensive evaluation of 20 diverse MLLMs (closed- and open-source) reveals a consistent and striking finding: many top models perform at or below random guessing on size/location tasks, which is a compelling and surprising empirical result supported by a large and controlled test set.

Useful ablation studies (number of shapes, visual encoder choice, noise injection, model scaling) provide some mechanistic insight into why models struggle (e.g., encoder positional embedding limitations, mixed-encoder degradation on spatial tasks), going beyond simple benchmark-and-report.

Downstream transfer experiment (LLaVA-GeP) trained on synthesized geometric perception data shows consistent (if modest) improvements on math/chart-related benchmarks, providing some evidence that the skill being measured has practical relevance beyond the synthetic benchmark itself.

Human evaluation (99.3% accuracy) with a reasonably described protocol establishes that the benchmark tasks are trivial for humans, strengthening the claim that failures reflect genuine model deficiencies rather than confusing or ill-posed questions.
Detailed appendices document model sources, prompts, hyperparameters, and evaluation/parsing procedures, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The benchmark relies entirely on synthetic, template-generated figures/questions with a template-based QA generation pipeline; this raises concerns about limited diversity in phrasing, potential answer/distractor artifacts, and whether performance reflects true 'geometric perception' versus overfitting to a narrow synthetic visual/textual distribution not representative of real-world imagery.

The downstream improvement from LLaVA-GeP training is small (average 2.2% on math/chart benchmarks) and is only demonstrated on a single base architecture (LLaVA-1.5-7B); no ablation isolates whether gains stem from the geometric perception content specifically versus simply additional visual instruction-tuning data/captions, weakening the causal claim that geometric perception is foundational for downstream tasks.

Human evaluation is conducted by only 5 undergraduate volunteers with minimal reported inter-rater/statistical detail, and each solved a relatively small subset per aspect; this is a fairly thin basis for claiming near-ceiling human performance as a rigorous baseline.

The paper does not report confidence intervals, variance, or statistical significance testing on the large performance gaps observed (e.g., below-random-guessing claims), which is important given multiple-choice guessing baselines and possible parsing/format sensitivity across very different model families.

Explanations for some counter-intuitive findings (e.g., noise sometimes improving accuracy; mixed encoders underperforming) are speculative post-hoc hypotheses without further experiments to substantiate them, limiting the mechanistic rigor of the analysis.

Only three closed-source models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-pro) are evaluated with a single fixed prompt and no exploration of prompting strategies (e.g., CoT, few-shot) that might substantially change performance, so the 'fundamental deficiency' claim may partly reflect zero-shot direct-answer brittleness rather than an inherent perceptual ceiling.

The relationship/reference/size categories rely on template-generated distractors, and the paper does not thoroughly analyze potential biases in distractor construction (e.g., systematic cues that let models exploit shortcuts rather than truly perceive geometry), which could inflate or deflate reported accuracies in ways not fully controlled for.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: existing MLLM benchmarks largely test high-level semantic understanding while ignoring low-level geometric perception, and the paper convincingly documents this gap via a human-vs-model comparison across 15 external benchmarks (Fig. 7).

The benchmark is large-scale (80K images, 285K QA pairs) and covers six clearly defined aspects (existence, counting, location, size, reference, relationship) with an automated, template-based data engine that ensures ground-truth consistency.

Broad evaluation of 20 closed- and open-source MLLMs reveals a striking and consistent weakness in spatial/size perception, including several models performing at or below random-guessing accuracy, which is a useful diagnostic finding for the community.

Human evaluation (99.3% accuracy) is included to validate that tasks are solvable and unambiguous, strengthening the claim that model failures reflect genuine perceptual deficits rather than task ambiguity.

Useful ablations (visual encoder choice, resolution, number of shapes, noise) provide some mechanistic insight, e.g., the counter-intuitive finding that mixed visual encoders hurt spatial accuracy despite helping on semantic tasks.
weaknesses: The benchmark is entirely synthetic (matplotlib-rendered abstract shapes), and the paper does not adequately justify or test whether performance on this narrow synthetic domain predicts geometric perception in the real-world applications it motivates (e.g., medical imaging, fossil classification); the claim of 'foundational' importance is asserted rather than demonstrated across realistic domains.

The related-work discussion focuses on math-reasoning geometry datasets (GeoQA, Geometry3K, etc.) but omits discussion/comparison with well-known synthetic compositional-scene benchmarks such as CLEVR, which test very similar primitives (existence, counting, relationships, spatial location) — this is a significant gap in positioning the contribution's novelty.

The downstream transfer results for LLaVA-GeP are weak and only partially supportive: the claimed 'general improvements' (avg +2.2% on math/chart benchmarks) are modest, and Figure 6 shows at least one benchmark (ChartBench) where LLaVA-GeP appears to underperform the LLaVA-1.5 baseline, which is not discussed or explained in the text, undermining the narrative of consistent benefit.

No ablation isolates whether gains from GePBench-derived training data come specifically from improved geometric/spatial perception versus simply added training-data volume/diversity (e.g., a control condition with an equal amount of non-geometric synthetic data is missing).

Some headline results (e.g., GPT-4o/Claude scoring below random guessing on 'size' questions) are surprising enough to warrant deeper error analysis or qualitative examples to rule out benchmark artifacts (e.g., systematic distractor bias, prompt formatting, or answer-parsing issues) rather than being reported at face value as evidence of perceptual failure.

Reproducibility is currently unverifiable: code and data are stated to be released ('will be publicly available') but were not provided with the submission, and prompts/exact distractor-generation heuristics for each aspect are only partially detailed.

The 'easy'/'hard' split is defined by a coarse heuristic (shape count >4 or noise presence) rather than by any calibrated measure of task difficulty, which limits the interpretability of the easy/hard breakdown in Table 1.

strengths: Identifies and addresses a genuine, underexplored gap: prior geometry datasets (GeoQA, Geometry3K, UniGeo, etc.) target long-chain mathematical reasoning rather than basic geometric perception, and GePBench isolates this foundational skill cleanly.

Large-scale, systematically constructed benchmark (80K images, 285K questions) with a controllable synthesis engine (structured description -> figure -> QA), enabling fine-grained control over difficulty (easy/hard via shape count and noise) and coverage of six well-motivated aspects (existence, counting, location, size, reference, relationship).

Extensive evaluation of 20 diverse closed- and open-source MLLMs, revealing consistent and sometimes striking deficiencies (e.g., GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet below random guessing on size questions), which is a compelling and surprising finding.
Human evaluation (99.3% accuracy) convincingly establishes that the tasks are trivial for humans, strengthening the claim of a genuine capability gap rather than a flawed or ambiguous benchmark.

Useful and diverse ablations: effect of shape count, visual encoder architecture/resolution, and image noise, offering some mechanistic insight (e.g., possible tension between translation/rotation-invariant encoders and precise spatial perception).

Downstream transfer experiment (LLaVA-GeP) shows that training on synthetic geometric perception data yields consistent, non-trivial improvements on both general benchmarks and math/chart-focused benchmarks, providing evidence of practical relevance beyond the benchmark itself.

Cross-benchmark comparison (Fig. 7) situating geometric perception relative to many other MLLM benchmarks in terms of human-model gap is a nice framing device that highlights the outsized difficulty of this ostensibly simple task.
weaknesses: The benchmark is entirely synthetic (matplotlib-rendered abstract shapes with template-generated questions/distractors); no analysis is provided on whether models could exploit dataset-specific artifacts (e.g., systematic distractor construction, answer-position biases, or text-only shortcuts). A blind/language-only baseline would help verify that visual perception, rather than answer-choice heuristics, drives the observed accuracy patterns, especially given the below-random-guessing results on size questions, which are unusual enough to warrant deeper diagnosis.

Ecological validity is unclear: it is not demonstrated that performance on these clean/noisy synthetic shapes correlates with geometric perception in real-world diagrams, medical images, or natural photographs, despite these being cited as key motivating applications.

The downstream benefit of GePBench-trained data is only shown for a single architecture (LLaVA-1.5-7B) and yields a fairly modest average gain (2.2% on math/chart benchmarks); it remains unclear whether the effect generalizes to stronger backbones or larger/more modern MLLMs, or whether it is driven mainly by increased instruction-tuning data volume rather than the specific geometric content.
The mixed-encoder and noise-impact analyses are interesting but their explanations (e.g., positional-embedding complexity from multiple encoders) are speculative and not directly tested or ablated.
The human-vs-model gap analysis in Section 4.4 mixes GPT-4o and GPT-4V results across different benchmarks and papers, introducing inconsistency into an otherwise appealing comparison.
Easy/hard categorization is coarse, based only on shape count threshold and presence/absence of noise, rather than a more principled or continuous difficulty measure.

Code and datasets are not yet released at submission time ("will be publicly available"), which limits current reproducibility, though this is a common and often acceptable practice pending acceptance.

The limitations section is brief and does not discuss the synthetic-to-real generalization gap or potential answer/shortcut biases, which are the more consequential limitations of this type of benchmark.
